title: Divisibility tests and modular remainders
transcript: A remainder measures how far a number is past a multiple. A remainder just one below the divisor tells you the number is one step before the next multiple. That one step can turn several awkward remainders into a single common multiples problem.

In AMC practice, read almost full groups and one short of a multiple as clues about a remainder. In a Rossmoyne style search, combine more than one remainder and use the interval to finish the argument.
Group sixty-four counters into packets of seven. How many counters remain outside full packets? Identify the last multiple of the packet size that fits. Then count the ungrouped counters.
nine packets use sixty-three counters. The next packet would bring the used total above sixty-four. Subtract to get one. The leftover amount is less than the group size, as a valid remainder must be.
Find the last digit of the three-digit number beginning with five and eight if the number is divisible by four and three. Use the last two digits for one test and the digit sum for the other.

The possible endings divisible by four are eighty, eighty-four and eighty-eight, so the last digit is zero, four or eight. The fixed digits sum to thirteen. Of those three last digits, only eight makes a multiple of three. The number is five hundred and eighty-eight. Its ending and its digit sum pass the two requested tests.

Count the numbers from seventy through two hundred and thirty-three whose remainder is five on division by six. The same numbers must give remainder eight on division by nine. What happens to both remainders if you add one?

Adding one to N makes it divisible by six and nine. Their least common multiple is eighteen. The shifted interval starts at seventy-one and ends at two hundred and thirty-four. Find the first and last multiples of eighteen in that interval. They start at seventy-two and finish at two hundred and thirty-four. Step by eighteen, including both ends.

There are nine steps between the endpoints. Include the first multiple to get ten numbers. Subtract one from each multiple to recover the original numbers. For example, the first is seventy-one and gives both required remainders.

A remainder can be zero, but it must always be smaller than the divisor. Once there are enough leftovers for a complete group, make that group. When you shift the number in a bounded search, shift the endpoints by the same amount. Pull each answer back to the original interval.

Name the divisor and the remainder together. Check whether adding or subtracting a small amount lands on a multiple. Check the first and last values against every condition. If you counted gaps, include the first valid value.
